summary: Specifies the Null Service, which allows applications to identify themselves to QoS policy agents using RSVP signaling without specifying resource requirements. Policy agents then apply appropriate policies.

plainLanguage.summary: An app can say who it is to the network without asking for any specific amount of speed, and the network picks the treatment.

questions: what is the rsvp null service type
how does rsvp work with diffserv
can rsvp be used without resource requirements
subtitle: How an application can tell the network who it is over RSVP without saying how much bandwidth it needs.

tldr.problem: Some applications are important to the network administrator but cannot say how many resources they need, so the usual RSVP and Intserv service types do not fit them.
tldr.mechanism: The Null Service Type lets a sender signal with RSVP that it asks for no specific service or quantity, while still identifying the user and application so that QoS policy agents can decide how to treat the traffic.
tldr.outcome: Policy agents can answer with a DCLASS object that tells the sender which DSCP to mark packets with. The RFC adds no new security issues beyond standard RSVP.

today: RFC 2997 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes how the Null Service fits with the diffserv and RSVP framework in RFC 2998.

sections.title: Why a Null Service Is Needed
sections.content:
With standard RSVP and Intserv signaling, a host tells the network four things: a requested service level (Guaranteed or Controlled Load), how many resources it needs at that level, classification information (a filterspec) that identifies the traffic, and policy information naming the user or application. Network nodes then admit or deny the request based on available resources and policy.

Some applications cannot, or choose not to, state their resource needs. The RFC gives enterprise resource planning (ERP) applications as an example: they are often mission critical and need prioritized service, but cannot readily specify requirements. Differentiated services (diffserv) suit them better, but diffserv has no signaling between hosts and the network.

That leaves administrators with two problems. Provisioning means guessing how much traffic will arrive for each behavior aggregate (BA). Classification means recognizing traffic by its diffserv codepoint (DSCP) or by multi-field (MF) matching on addresses, ports and protocol, which the RFC calls potentially unreliable and a management burden. Using RSVP signaling can make this management significantly easier.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs matter a lot but cannot say how much speed they need. The old way of asking for speed does not work for them, so the network has to guess.

sections.title: How the Null Service Works
sections.content:
The RSVP sender offers a new service type, the Null Service Type, in the ADSPEC carried in its PATH message. A matching new Tspec is added to the SENDER_TSPEC. The sender will typically also include policy objects that identify the user, the application and a sub application ID.

Network nodes read the Null Service as a request for no specific service type and no quantifiable resources. They manage the flow by user, application and type of sub-flow instead.

Even so, the signaling tells each interested node how many flows of a particular type pass through it, and which user, application and sub-application the classification information belongs to. Policy enforcement points (PEPs) and policy decision points (PDPs) can use this to apply the administrator's policy.

A PEP or PDP may return an RSVP RESV message that carries a DCLASS object. This tells the sender to mark packets on that flow with a specific DSCP (or set of DSCPs), which lets policy shape how much traffic reaches a node for any given BA.
sections.plainLanguage: The program says who it is and which job it does. The network then tells it which lane to use on the road.

sections.title: Signaling Details
sections.content:
The sender builds an initial ADSPEC naming the Null Service Type. Because the service has no parameters, its ADSPEC fragment is empty and holds only the header word. Nodes may not supply real values for bandwidth and latency, and may use the unknown values defined in RFC 2216.

The new Tspec goes in the SENDER_TSPEC object. If only the Null Service is offered, it is the only Tspec. If Guaranteed or Controlled Load is offered too, the new Tspec is appended after the standard Intserv token-bucket Tspec from RFC 2210. At this time the new Tspec carries only one parameter, the maximum packet size (M), which is there to avoid fragmentation.

Receivers may answer PATH messages with a RESV message containing a FLOWSPEC object. That FLOWSPEC should specify that it is requesting the Null Service. The RFC notes that a specific Rspec may be defined for it in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender fills in a form that says only who it is. The receiver writes back on the same kind of form.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
The Null Service ADSPEC is the usual message header and default general parameters fragment, followed by one extra fragment for the Null Service. That fragment is a single header word: service number 6, a break bit, reserved bits, and a length of 0 words beyond the header.

Old network elements are safe. Under the standard ADSPEC parsing rules, an element that does not understand a per-service header sets bit 23 (the break bit) to show the service is unsupported and uses the length field to skip the rest of the fragment.

The Null Service Tspec has service number 6, a per-service data length of 2 words, and a single parameter, ID 128 (Null Service TSpec), with length 1 word holding the Maximum Packet Size [M] as a 32-bit integer. The FLOWSPEC mirrors this, with service header number 6 and the same parameter 128. DCLASS object details are left to RFC 2996.
sections.plainLanguage: The form is very short. It has a label saying Null Service and one box for the biggest package size.

sections.title: Scalability and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
Per-flow signaling raises scalability concerns, and the Null Service encourages signaling for more applications than before. The RFC argues that RSVP signaling is small relative to the data traffic of a session, and that the Null Service should be used only by applications considered mission critical or needing QoS management by administrators.

Processing load at nodes is the bigger worry. It is not necessary to process signaling at every node: key nodes such as domain boundaries, first-hop routers or PEPs may be enough, and RSVP processing is enabled or disabled per node at the administrator's discretion. Per-flow state is not necessarily required, even in nodes that do per-flow processing.

Nodes that follow the RSVP spec should pass Null Service messages along transparently, so a few Null-Service-enabled PEPs can be added to a legacy network. An application may also offer a quantitative Intserv service and the Null Service together, as a telephony application might, letting network policy choose.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a few checkpoints need to read the notes. The rest of the roads just let the notes pass through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the message formatting and usage rules raise no new security issues beyond standard RSVP. It adds no other security text.

The user, application and sub application identity carried in the policy objects come from other specifications, RFC 2752 and RFC 2872.
sections.plainLanguage: This idea is as safe as the system it builds on, and it does not add new dangers.
